title: The RBI Just Cut the Cost of Bringing Dollars Home. NRIs, This One Is for You.
excerpt: A concessional forex swap at half the market rate, leverage on NRI deposits, and a $50–70 billion inflow target — India's central bank is pulling every lever to defend the rupee.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India has done something it last attempted in 2013, and the signal is unmistakable: it wants your dollars.

On Monday, the RBI published detailed guidelines for a concessional forex swap facility — one of several measures announced on Friday to shore up the rupee after it hit a new low against the dollar last month. The swap will be offered at a fixed rate of 1.5% per annum, roughly half the prevailing forward premium of 2.5–3%. The facility is open until January 15, 2027, covering borrowings raised through December 31.

The immediate beneficiaries are public sector undertakings raising external commercial borrowings (ECBs) of three years or more. But the bigger play is aimed squarely at the Indian diaspora.

## The NRI Deposit Push

The RBI has also opened a parallel scheme for fresh Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR-B) deposits. Banks can now mobilise deposits in any freely convertible currency, with a one-year lock-in period, and swap them into rupees at the concessional rate through September 30.

The critical addition: banks can now offer leverage on these deposits. The RBI has removed restrictions on banks issuing standby letters of credit to foreign banks, allowing them to extend leverage to NRI customers parking dollars in Indian banks. When the RBI last offered this in 2013, the leverage provision was the single most important driver of inflows.

Jefferies estimates the combined measures — concessional swaps, NRI deposit leverage, and overseas borrowing incentives — could bring in $50 billion to $70 billion. Citi Research called the leverage provision "an additional announcement" that markets had not fully priced in after Friday's initial release.

## Why Now

The arithmetic is straightforward. India's oil-and-gas import bill jumped 53% in April from March. HSBC had expected the balance of payments deficit to swell to $65 billion in fiscal 2027; it now expects the RBI's measures to improve the balance by about $30 billion. The rupee closed at 95.35 per dollar on Tuesday, up 0.4% for the session after oil prices fell on the Iran–Israel ceasefire.

But the structural pressure is unrelenting. Foreign investors have sold Indian equities for seven consecutive sessions. Interest rate swap markets are pricing in at least 25 basis points of rate hikes over the next three months. ICICI Securities said the measures should improve banks' liability profiles by increasing the share of stable medium-term foreign currency deposits — a direct response to the deposit mobilisation challenge banks have faced as households shift savings into equities.

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs holding dollars in overseas accounts, the math has shifted. Indian banks can now effectively offer a subsidised return on dollar deposits, backstopped by the RBI's concessional swap window. The 1.5% swap rate means the cost of converting those dollars into rupee-denominated assets has halved.

The last time India ran this playbook, in 2013, it raised over $34 billion in FCNR deposits within months — a sum widely credited with stabilising the rupee during that year's taper tantrum. The stakes this time are higher: India is not dealing with sentiment-driven capital flight but with a physical disruption to its oil supply that shows no sign of resolving quickly.

Barclays said the measures will alleviate some of the pressure on the rupee but warned that the current account deficit "remains heavily oil-driven." The rupee is likely on a depreciating path, "albeit at a much more gradual pace than in past months."

For the 32 million-strong Indian diaspora, the RBI's message is plain: park your dollars in India, and we will make it worth your while. Whether the diaspora responds as it did in 2013 will determine how much runway India buys itself in a war it did not start.
